etymology: From Latin murmurare, to make a low sound; the word is onomatopoeic. Webster 1828: to grumble; to complain; to utter complaints in a low, half-articulated voice. In Scripture it is the characteristic sin of the wilderness generation, and the New Testament forbids it to the church by name.
biblical_def: Murmured is the wilderness verb. Three days out of the Red Sea, the people murmured against Moses, saying, What shall we drink? (Exodus 15:24). At the wilderness of Sin the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron (Exodus 16:2). After Korah’s judgment, all the congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron, saying, Ye have killed the people of the LORD (Numbers 16:41). And God treats it as directed at Himself: Your carcases shall fall in this wilderness… which have murmured against me (Numbers 14:29). Deuteronomy records what murmuring actually says when it is quoted: ye murmured in your tents, and said, Because the LORD hated us, he hath brought us forth out of the land of Egypt (Deuteronomy 1:27) — the recasting of deliverance as malice. The psalm summarizes: But murmured in their tents, and hearkened not unto the voice of the LORD (Psalm 106:25). In the Gospels the Jews then murmured at him, because he said, I am the bread which came down from heaven (John 6:41). Paul makes the wilderness the church’s warning: Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer (1 Corinthians 10:10).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MURMUR as a low sound continued or continually repeated; and, as a verb, to grumble, to complain, to utter complaints in a low, half-articulated voice. The half-articulated quality is exactly the sin’s character.
webster_full: MURMUR, n. — A low sound continued or continually repeated, as that of a stream running in a stony channel.
A complaint half suppressed, or uttered in a low, muttering voice.
MURMUR, v.i. — To utter complaints in a low, half-articulated voice; to grumble; to express discontent.

The definition catches what makes murmuring so hard to deal with pastorally. It is not open rebellion, which can be answered, but a low continual sound in the tents that never becomes an argument anyone has to defend.
scriptures: Exodus 16:2
And the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness:
Numbers 14:29
Your carcases shall fall in this wilderness; and all that were numbered of you, according to your whole number, from twenty years old and upward, which have murmured against me,
Deuteronomy 1:27
And ye murmured in your tents, and said, Because the LORD hated us, he hath brought us forth out of the land of Egypt, to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us.
John 6:41
The Jews then murmured at him, because he said, I am the bread which came down from heaven.
1 Corinthians 10:10
Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer.
corruption_summary: Murmuring is corrupted into a virtue wherever complaint is renamed as honesty, authenticity, or the healthy processing of disappointment — and 1 Corinthians 10:10 shows the apostolic estimate of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 14:29 makes the decisive point: Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, and God says they murmured against me. Complaint about circumstances is complaint about the Providence that arranged them, whatever name it travels under. The contemporary permission to vent, to be raw, to say the unedited thing as though sincerity sanctified it, has no footing in these chapters. Scripture provides an abundant vocabulary for honest grief before God — the psalms of lament are in the canon and are meant to be prayed — but a lament is addressed to God and ends in trust, while a murmur is spoken in the tents about Him. Deuteronomy 1:27 quotes what it actually said: Because the LORD hated us. That is the theology inside every murmur.

Paul’s warning in 1 Corinthians 10:10 is addressed to a church, not to Israel, and the whole passage says these things are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come. The remedy he gives elsewhere is startlingly absolute: Do all things without murmurings and disputings (Philippians 2:14) — and the verse before it grounds the possibility in grace, it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure. A congregation where discontent circulates quietly is not merely unpleasant; it is repeating the sin for which a generation’s carcases fell in the wilderness. Isaiah adds the hope: they that murmured shall learn doctrine (Isaiah 29:24). The cure for a murmuring people is teaching.
roots_summary: The Hebrew verb is lun, to lodge or to grumble — the same root as spending the night, which is why murmuring in Scripture is done in tents. The Greek gogguzo is itself an imitation of the sound.
roots_lines: Hebrew lun (H3885) — to lodge, to pass the night, and in a related form to murmur or grumble; Exodus 15:24, 16:2, Numbers 14:29.
Hebrew ragan (H7279) — to backbite, to murmur; ye murmured in your tents (Deuteronomy 1:27; Psalm 106:25).
Greek gogguzo (G1111) — to mutter, murmur; an onomatopoeic verb (John 6:41; 1 Corinthians 10:10).
Greek goggusmos (G1112) — murmuring; Do all things without murmurings and disputings (Philippians 2:14).
The overlap of lun as lodging and grumbling is not accidental in the narrative: the murmuring is done in the tents, at night, out of Moses’ hearing.
usage: Which have murmured against me (Numbers 14:29) — God receives complaint against His servants as complaint against Himself.
Ye murmured in your tents, and said, Because the LORD hated us (Deuteronomy 1:27) — the theology hidden inside a murmur, quoted back.
Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured (1 Corinthians 10:10) — the wilderness written for the church’s admonition.

etymology: From over plus throw. Webster 1828: to turn upside down; to demolish; to defeat and ruin. In the Authorized Version it is the standing word for the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, for the command to demolish Canaanite altars, and for the ruin the wicked plot against the righteous.
biblical_def: Overthrow in Scripture is a turning upside down that leaves nothing standing. It is the fixed term for Sodom: Lot pleads for Zoar and is told I will not overthrow this city (Genesis 19:21), and the record of the judgment names it twice in one verse — God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in the which Lot dwelt (Genesis 19:29). The same verb is commanded of Israel toward the gods of Canaan: Thou shalt not bow down to their gods, nor serve them, nor do after their works: but thou shalt utterly overthrow them, and quite break down their images (Exodus 23:24) — not tolerate, not relocate, but demolish. It also describes God’s judgment on His own people when they refused the land: he lifted up his hand against them, to overthrow them in the wilderness (Psalm 106:26). And it names what the wicked intend: preserve me from the violent man; who have purposed to overthrow my goings (Psalm 140:4), and the corrupt court that would overthrow the righteous in judgment (Proverbs 18:5). The word therefore covers the two great overturnings — what God does to entrenched wickedness, and what wickedness attempts against the righteous and cannot finish.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives OVERTHROW as to turn upside down; to throw down; to demolish; to ruin; to defeat; and as a noun, the state of being overturned, ruin, destruction, defeat.
webster_full: OVERTHROW, v.t. — To turn upside down; as, to overthrow a carriage.
To throw down; to demolish; to destroy; as, to overthrow a building; to overthrow a government.
To defeat; to conquer; to vanquish; as, to overthrow an army.
OVERTHROW, n. — The state of being overturned or turned off the basis; ruin; destruction; defeat; discomfiture.
Webster’s first sense — turned off the basis — is the biblical picture. Sodom was not damaged; it was overturned, and the plain where it stood is the standing witness.
scriptures: Genesis 19:21
And he said unto him, See, I have accepted thee concerning this thing also, that I will not overthrow this city, for the which thou hast spoken.
Genesis 19:29
And it came to pass, when God destroyed the cities of the plain, that God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in the which Lot dwelt.
Exodus 23:24
Thou shalt not bow down to their gods, nor serve them, nor do after their works: but thou shalt utterly overthrow them, and quite break down their images.
Psalm 106:26
Therefore he lifted up his hand against them, to overthrow them in the wilderness:
Proverbs 18:5
It is not good to accept the person of the wicked, to overthrow the righteous in judgment.
corruption_summary: The overthrow of Sodom is corrupted when it is reinterpreted as a judgment on inhospitality alone, detaching it from the sin the rest of Scripture names — and the command of Exodus 23:24 is corrupted whenever the church negotiates with idols it was told to break.
corruption_paragraphs: The revisionist reading of Genesis 19 makes the overthrow a judgment on the violation of hospitality, appealing to Ezekiel 16:49. Ezekiel does list pride, fulness of bread, and neglect of the poor — and then adds in the next verse, they were haughty, and committed abomination before me: therefore I took them away as I saw good. The New Testament settles the matter without ambiguity: Sodom and Gomorrah, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire (Jude 7), and Peter makes the overthrow the pattern of God’s dealing with the ungodly (2 Peter 2:6). Scripture’s own commentary on Scripture is the standard here, and it names both the pride and the abomination rather than trading one for the other.

Exodus 23:24 is the harder command for a comfortable church. Israel was not told to ignore the Canaanite gods or to reinterpret them charitably but to utterly overthrow them, and quite break down their images. The New Testament does not hand the church a crowbar — our weapons are not carnal — but it keeps the demand for demolition: casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ (2 Corinthians 10:5). Idols in a believer’s life are not managed, reduced, or kept at a safe distance. Josiah’s reformation is the Old Testament picture and Ephesus’s bonfire of curious books is the New; in both, something was destroyed that could have been sold.
roots_summary: The Hebrew haphak means to turn over or overturn, and its noun mahpekah is the standing term for the overthrow of the cities of the plain; the same root gives the idea of a thing turned upside down.
roots_lines: Hebrew haphak (H2015) — to turn, overturn, overthrow; Genesis 19:21, 29; Psalm 106:26.
Hebrew mahpekah (H4114) — an overthrow, a catastrophe; the fixed noun for the destruction of Sodom, used by Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Amos as a byword.
Hebrew harac (H2040) — to break down, tear down; quite break down their images (Exodus 23:24).
Greek katastrophe (G2692) — an overthrow; used by Peter of the cities turning into ashes (2 Peter 2:6), and the source of English catastrophe.
The prophets use as the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah as a fixed simile for total judgment (Isaiah 13:19; Jeremiah 49:18; Amos 4:11).
usage: Sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow (Genesis 19:29) — deliverance recorded as an act of remembering Abraham.
Thou shalt utterly overthrow them, and quite break down their images (Exodus 23:24) — demolition commanded, not accommodation.
To overthrow the righteous in judgment (Proverbs 18:5) — the corruption of a court described in the same verb as the ruin of Sodom.

etymology: From the Italian all' arme, to arms. Webster 1828: any sound, outcry or information intended to give notice of approaching danger; a summons to arms. In the Authorized Version the alarm is a specific trumpet signal, distinguished by God Himself from the ordinary call to assemble.
biblical_def: God gave Israel two silver trumpets and two signals, and He distinguished them. When ye blow an alarm, then the camps that lie on the east parts shall go forward (Numbers 10:5); when ye blow an alarm the second time, then the camps that lie on the south side shall take their journey (Numbers 10:6). Then the crucial verse: But when the congregation is to be gathered together, ye shall blow, but ye shall not sound an alarm (Numbers 10:7). The same instrument, played two ways, calls a people to move out or to come in, and the difference is not left to the trumpeter’s taste. The prophets take the alarm as the sound of the day of the LORD. Jeremiah cannot bear it: my heart maketh a noise in me; I cannot hold my peace, because thou hast heard, O my soul, the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war (Jeremiah 4:19). Joel makes it the summons to repentance: Blow ye the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain: let all the inhabitants of the land tremble: for the day of the LORD cometh (Joel 2:1). Zephaniah names the day itself a day of the trumpet and alarm against the fenced cities, and against the high towers (Zephaniah 1:16).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ALARM as any sound, outcry or information intended to give notice of approaching danger; a summons to arms; and the sudden fear or apprehension excited by such notice.
webster_full: ALARM, n. [It. all' arme, to arms.] — Any sound, outcry or information intended to give notice of approaching danger; as, to sound an alarm.
A summons to arms; the call by which men are aroused to defence.
Sudden surprise with fear or terror; also, terror; a sensation excited by an apprehension of danger.
The Italian origin is a shouted command, and that is the biblical function. An alarm is not an atmosphere of anxiety; it is a signal with a specified meaning that requires a specified response.
scriptures: Numbers 10:5
When ye blow an alarm, then the camps that lie on the east parts shall go forward.
Numbers 10:6
When ye blow an alarm the second time, then the camps that lie on the south side shall take their journey: they shall blow an alarm for their journeys.
Numbers 10:7
But when the congregation is to be gathered together, ye shall blow, but ye shall not sound an alarm.
Jeremiah 4:19
My bowels, my bowels! I am pained at my very heart; my heart maketh a noise in me; I cannot hold my peace, because thou hast heard, O my soul, the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war.
Joel 2:1
Blow ye the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain: let all the inhabitants of the land tremble: for the day of the LORD cometh, for it is nigh at hand;
corruption_summary: The alarm is corrupted in two ways: by pulpits that never sound one, so that the day of the LORD is announced to nobody; and by ministries that sound nothing else, so that a congregation is kept perpetually agitated and learns to ignore the trumpet.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 10:7 is a rebuke to the second error before it is a rebuke to the first. When the congregation is merely to be gathered, ye shall blow, but ye shall not sound an alarm. God distinguishes between calling His people together and calling them to war, and He forbids using the war signal for the ordinary summons. A ministry that treats every issue as an emergency, every cultural development as the last crisis, and every sermon as a call to arms has broken this ordinance, and the practical result is that when a real alarm comes the camp does not move. Paul makes the same point about clarity: if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle? (1 Corinthians 14:8).

The opposite failure is the more common in comfortable churches. Joel 2:1 commands the alarm precisely because the day of the LORD is at hand, and the chapter goes on to the great call, turn ye even to me with all your heart, with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning. Jeremiah 4:19 shows what it costs a man to be the trumpet: he is pained at his very heart and cannot hold his peace. A preacher who has never felt that has probably never sounded it. Ezekiel sets the watchman’s duty and the penalty for silence side by side — if the watchman sees the sword come and blows not the trumpet, the people’s blood is required at his hand (Ezekiel 33:6).
roots_summary: The Hebrew terua' is a shout or blast, the same noun used of the shout at Jericho and of the joyful blast on the day of the trumpets; its verb means to raise a shout.
roots_lines: Hebrew terua' (H8643) — a shout, blast, alarm; the trumpet signal of Numbers 10:5-7 and the sound of Joel 2:1.
Hebrew rua' (H7321) — to raise a shout, to sound an alarm; the verb behind the noun, and the shout at Jericho.
Hebrew chatsotserah (H2689) — the silver trumpet of Numbers 10, distinct from the ram’s-horn shophar.
Hebrew yom terua' — the day of blowing of trumpets (Numbers 29:1), where the same noun names a feast rather than a warning.
Greek salpigx (G4536) — a trumpet; behind if the trumpet give an uncertain sound (1 Corinthians 14:8) and the last trump of 1 Corinthians 15:52.
usage: When ye blow an alarm, then the camps… shall go forward (Numbers 10:5) — a signal with a fixed meaning and a required response.
Ye shall blow, but ye shall not sound an alarm (Numbers 10:7) — God forbids using the war signal for the ordinary summons.
Sound an alarm in my holy mountain: for the day of the LORD cometh (Joel 2:1) — the alarm as a call to national repentance.

etymology: From wonder plus the adjectival ending. Webster 1828: admirable; marvellous; such as may excite surprise and astonishment; strange. In the Authorized Version it is fixed almost entirely in one phrase — thy wondrous works — and it is the standing object of the church’s song and speech.
biblical_def: Wondrous in Scripture attaches to God’s works and is nearly always paired with an act of telling. David’s psalm at the bringing of the ark commands it: Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him, talk ye of all his wondrous works (1 Chronicles 16:9), repeated word for word in the psalter (Psalm 105:2). The vow is personal: That I may publish with the voice of thanksgiving, and tell of all thy wondrous works (Psalm 26:7), and generational: O God, thou hast taught me from my youth: and hitherto have I declared thy wondrous works (Psalm 71:17). The doxology of Book Two closes with it: Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel, who only doeth wondrous things (Psalm 72:18) — the only is the point, since no rival works them. Asaph says thou art great, and doest wondrous things: thou art God alone (Psalm 86:10), and Psalm 75:1 gives the reason for thanksgiving: for that thy name is near thy wondrous works declare. The dark verse is the one that must be kept beside them: For all this they sinned still, and believed not for his wondrous works (Psalm 78:32). Wonders do not produce faith. Israel saw the sea open and murmured within three days.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WONDROUS as admirable; marvellous; such as may excite surprise and astonishment; strange. The KJV binds it to God’s works, and always in the context of declaring them.
webster_full: WONDROUS, a. — Admirable; marvellous; such as may excite surprise and astonishment; strange.
WONDER, n. — That emotion which is excited by novelty, or the presentation of some object which is unusual or beyond the ordinary course of nature.
Also, a cause of wonder; a prodigy; a miracle.
The English word carries the reaction, but the Hebrew behind the biblical phrase describes the deed itself — something too high, too extraordinary, for a man to do or to comprehend.
scriptures: 1 Chronicles 16:9
Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him, talk ye of all his wondrous works.
Psalm 26:7
That I may publish with the voice of thanksgiving, and tell of all thy wondrous works.
Psalm 72:18
Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel, who only doeth wondrous things.
Psalm 78:32
For all this they sinned still, and believed not for his wondrous works.
Psalm 86:10
For thou art great, and doest wondrous things: thou art God alone.
corruption_summary: The word is corrupted where wonder is detached from the God who works it — a taste for the spectacular that leaves the worshipper unchanged — and Psalm 78:32 is the Bible’s own verdict on that arrangement.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 78:32 is the standing refutation of every ministry built on signs. Israel had seen the plagues, the sea, the manna, the rock, and the cloud, and the psalm reports flatly: For all this they sinned still, and believed not for his wondrous works. Miracles are real, God works them, and they authenticate revelation — but they do not regenerate. Our Lord said as much through Abraham in the parable: If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead (Luke 16:31). Where a movement makes the pursuit of the miraculous the centre of its life, it has arranged its ministry around the one thing Psalm 78 says did not produce faith in the generation that saw the most of it.

The positive command is what should replace it, and it is repeated: talk ye of all his wondrous works. The wondrous works are to be sung, published with thanksgiving, and declared from youth to age, which is a description of ordinary Christian worship and ordinary family instruction rather than of an event. Psalm 72:18 fixes the boundary that keeps it from becoming vague awe: it is the LORD God, the God of Israel, who only doeth wondrous things. Wonder without that name is available anywhere — in nature, in art, in the night sky — and it saves nobody. The psalmists never wonder in the abstract; they always name Him.
roots_summary: The Hebrew root pala' means to be extraordinary, surpassing, too high for a man; its participle gives wondrous works, and its noun form is the Wonderful of Isaiah 9:6.
roots_lines: Hebrew pala' (H6381) — to be marvellous, surpassing, beyond a man’s power; its participle gives wondrous works throughout the psalms.
Hebrew niphla'oth — wondrous things, marvellous works; the standing plural noun (1 Chronicles 16:9; Psalm 26:7; Psalm 105:2).
Hebrew pele (H6382) — a wonder; the name given the Child in Isaiah 9:6, his name shall be called Wonderful.
Hebrew 'oth and mopheth — sign and wonder; the pair used of the exodus miracles, which Psalm 78 says did not produce faith.
Greek thaumasios (G2297) — wonderful; the children’s cry in the temple over the wonderful things that he did (Matthew 21:15).
usage: Talk ye of all his wondrous works (1 Chronicles 16:9) — the works are given to be spoken of, not merely admired.
Who only doeth wondrous things (Psalm 72:18) — the exclusivity that keeps wonder from becoming vague.
They sinned still, and believed not for his wondrous works (Psalm 78:32) — miracles do not produce faith.

etymology: Old English slumerian, to doze. Webster 1828: to sleep lightly; to doze; also, to be in a state of negligence or inactivity. Scripture uses it for three different things — what God never does, what the sluggard loves, and what God judicially gives to those who will not see.
biblical_def: The first thing Scripture says about slumber is that God does not. He will not suffer thy foot to be moved: he that keepeth thee will not slumber. Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep (Psalm 121:3-4). The pilgrim looking up at the hills is told that the watch over him is unbroken, which is the doctrine of preservation stated as a night watch. The second use is the sluggard’s. Proverbs mocks him in a refrain repeated twice: Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep (Proverbs 6:10; 24:33), and the poverty that follows comes as one that travelleth. Against that, David’s vow for the house of God: I will not give sleep to mine eyes, or slumber to mine eyelids (Psalm 132:4), and wisdom’s urgency in a matter of debt, Give not sleep to thine eyes, nor slumber to thine eyelids (Proverbs 6:4). The third use is judicial and terrible. Isaiah’s watchmen are blind… dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber (Isaiah 56:10), and Paul quotes the Old Testament of unbelieving Israel: God hath given them the spirit of slumber, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear (Romans 11:8).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SLUMBER as to sleep lightly; to doze; and figuratively, to be in a state of negligence, sloth, or inactivity. All three biblical uses fall inside that definition.
webster_full: SLUMBER, v.i. — To sleep lightly; to doze.
To be in a state of negligence, sloth, supineness or inactivity.
SLUMBER, n. — Light sleep; sleep not deep or sound.
Repose; inactivity.

Webster’s second sense is the one Proverbs and Isaiah exploit. The sluggard and the blind watchman are not accused of resting; they are accused of a light, comfortable inattention while something was required of them.
scriptures: Psalm 121:3
He will not suffer thy foot to be moved: he that keepeth thee will not slumber.
Psalm 121:4
Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.
Proverbs 6:10
Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep:
Isaiah 56:10
His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber.
Romans 11:8
(According as it is written, God hath given them the spirit of slumber, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear;) unto this day.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The pressure is practical: Psalm 121 is quoted for comfort while Isaiah 56:10 is never quoted at all, so that God’s sleeplessness is preached to a church whose watchmen are asleep.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nobody is contesting the word. What has happened is a selection. Psalm 121 is among the best-loved passages in the psalter and is rightly preached — the God who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps, and a believer’s security rests on a watch that is never handed over. That is the doctrine of preservation, and it is the ground of perseverance: the saints continue because the Keeper does not doze.

Isaiah 56:10 is the verse that goes unread beside it, and it is aimed at ministers. The watchmen are blind, ignorant, and dumb dogs, they cannot bark, and the charge against them is that they love to slumber. A dog that will not bark is not gentle; it is useless, and the flock is unwarned. Romans 11:8 raises the stakes further, since there a spirit of slumber is God’s judicial act on a people who would not see. That combination — a God who never sleeps, watchmen who love to, and a slumber that can be given as judgment — is the whole doctrine in this word, and only the first third of it is commonly preached.
roots_summary: The Hebrew num means to be drowsy; its noun tenumah is the light sleep of the sluggard. The Greek katanuxis in Romans 11:8 means a stupor or deep numbness.
roots_lines: Hebrew num (H5123) — to slumber, be drowsy; he that keepeth thee will not slumber (Psalm 121:3-4), loving to slumber (Isaiah 56:10).
Hebrew tenumah (H8572) — slumber, drowsiness; the sluggard’s a little slumber (Proverbs 6:10; 24:33) and David’s vow (Psalm 132:4).
Hebrew yashen (H3462) — to sleep; the deeper word paired with num in Psalm 121:4 for emphasis.
Greek katanuxis (G2659) — a stupor, deep numbness; the spirit of slumber (Romans 11:8), quoting Isaiah 29:10.
Greek nustazo (G3573) — to nod, to be drowsy; the ten virgins all slumbered and slept (Matthew 25:5).
usage: He that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep (Psalm 121:4) — preservation stated as an unbroken night watch.
A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands (Proverbs 6:10) — the sluggard’s ruin arrives in small instalments.
Dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber (Isaiah 56:10) — the charge against watchmen who will not warn.

etymology: Old English flor. Webster 1828: that part of a building on which we walk; also, a threshing floor, a level area for treading out grain. In the Authorized Version the second sense carries most of the weight: the threshingfloor is where grain is separated from chaff, and it becomes a figure of judgment.
biblical_def: The floor in Scripture is usually a threshingfloor, a hard level place where the harvest is beaten and winnowed. It stands for the yield of a man’s labour: a released servant is to be furnished out of thy flock, and out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress (Deuteronomy 15:14). It is where Ruth goes at Naomi’s direction — get thee down to the floor (Ruth 3:3) — and where Boaz, guarding her reputation as carefully as her claim, says Let it not be known that a woman came into the floor (Ruth 3:14). It also names the literal floor of holy places: dust that is in the floor of the tabernacle was used in the trial of jealousy (Numbers 5:17), and Solomon overlaid the floor of the house with gold, within and without (1 Kings 6:30). But the figure that governs is John the Baptist’s. Of the Coming One he says, Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matthew 3:12). The threshingfloor is the visible church and the world alike, wheat and chaff lying together until the winnowing fan comes into a hand that will not tire.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives FLOOR as that part of a building or room on which we walk; and, secondly, a platform of boards or planks laid on timbers, as also the pavement or level area on which grain is threshed. Scripture uses both.
webster_full: FLOOR, n. — That part of a building or room on which we walk; the bottom or lower part, consisting of boards, planks or pavement.
A platform of boards or planks laid on timbers, as in a bridge; also, the area on which corn is threshed — a threshing floor.
FLOOR, v.t. — To lay a floor; to cover with a floor.

The threshing floor of the ancient world was an open, hard, level place, often on a height where the wind could carry off the chaff — which is why the winnowing image and the wind belong together in Scripture.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 15:14
Thou shalt furnish him liberally out of thy flock, and out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress: of that wherewith the LORD thy God hath blessed thee thou shalt give unto him.
Ruth 3:6
And she went down unto the floor, and did according to all that her mother in law bade her.
Ruth 3:14
And she lay at his feet until the morning: and she rose up before one could know another. And he said, Let it not be known that a woman came into the floor.
1 Kings 6:30
And the floor of the house he overlaid with gold, within and without.
Matthew 3:12
Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.
corruption_summary: Matthew 3:12 is corrupted whenever the winnowing is domesticated — the fan made a metaphor for personal refinement rather than a separation of persons — and Ruth 3 whenever the threshingfloor scene is read as a seduction rather than as the careful legal claim it is.
corruption_paragraphs: John the Baptist’s sentence has three parts and modern preaching keeps two. The Coming One will purge His floor, gather His wheat into the garner, and burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire. The purging is a separation of persons, not a purification of a single person’s character — the wheat goes one way and the chaff the other, and both destinations are named. Where the figure is softened into a general account of God refining His people, John’s warning is lost, and with it the reason he was preaching repentance to a crowd that thought Abrahamic descent settled the question. The visible church is a threshingfloor: wheat and chaff lie on it together now, and the fan is in a hand already raised.

Ruth 3 requires the opposite correction. The scene is read prurient by modern commentators and preached nervously by those who have absorbed them, but the text itself is scrupulous. Naomi sends Ruth to claim the kinsman-redeemer’s duty; Ruth asks Boaz to spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid; for thou art a near kinsman; and Boaz answers by blessing her, promising to perform the part of a kinsman, and protecting her reputation before dawn — Let it not be known that a woman came into the floor (Ruth 3:14). Then he goes to the gate and does it legally, in public, before witnesses. The chapter is a model of how a godly man handles a woman’s vulnerability and a legal claim at once: with kindness, with restraint, and in the open.
roots_summary: The Hebrew goren is a threshingfloor; the Greek halon in Matthew 3:12 is the same, an open threshing area. The English word covers both the household floor and the threshing floor, as the Hebrew and Greek do not.
roots_lines: Hebrew goren (H1637) — a threshingfloor; Deuteronomy 15:14, Ruth 3:3-14, and the floor of Araunah the Jebusite that became the temple site.
Hebrew qarqa' (H7172) — the floor or bottom of a building; the floor of the tabernacle (Numbers 5:17) and of Solomon’s house (1 Kings 6:30).
Greek halon (G257) — a threshingfloor; he will throughly purge his floor (Matthew 3:12; Luke 3:17).
Greek ptuon (G4425) — a winnowing fan or fork; the instrument in the Coming One’s hand.
Greek apotheke (G596) — a storehouse, garner; where the wheat is gathered, set against the unquenchable fire for the chaff.
usage: Out of thy flock, and out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress (Deuteronomy 15:14) — the floor as the measure of a man’s increase, and of his liberality.
Let it not be known that a woman came into the floor (Ruth 3:14) — a redeemer guarding the reputation of the woman he intends to marry.
He will throughly purge his floor (Matthew 3:12) — the winnowing that separates wheat from chaff, with both destinations named.

etymology: From dry, Old English drygan. Webster 1828: freed from moisture; exsiccated. In the Authorized Version the word marks the great acts of God over water — the flood receding, the Red sea, the Jordan — and also the failing of a brook that taught a prophet to trust the God who dried it.
biblical_def: Dried in Scripture is usually God acting on water. After the flood the raven went to and fro until the waters were dried up from off the earth (Genesis 8:7), and in due time was the earth dried (Genesis 8:14). At the Jordan Joshua tells the nation why the stones were set up: the LORD your God dried up the waters of Jordan from before you, until ye were passed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red sea, which he dried up from before us (Joshua 4:23). Two generations, two waters, one God who dries a path for His people. The word also marks judgment and testing. Israel in the wilderness complains, our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes (Numbers 11:6) — contempt for daily bread. Samson’s green withs were never dried (Judges 16:7), the first of his careless bargains with his own strength. And Elijah, fed by ravens at Cherith, learns the harder lesson: it came to pass after a while, that the brook dried up, because there had been no rain in the land (1 Kings 17:7) — the same drought he had announced, reaching him, and sending him on to the widow of Zarephath.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DRIED as freed from moisture or made dry; exsiccated. The KJV uses it above all of waters God removes to make a way, and of streams He allows to fail.
webster_full: DRIED, pp. of DRY — Freed from moisture or sap; exsiccated.
DRY, v.t. — To free from water or moisture; to exsiccate; to drain.
DRY, a. — Destitute of moisture; free from water or wetness; arid; not moist.
The passive participle in Scripture almost always has God as its agent, whether stated or implied. The waters do not simply recede; they are dried up from before a people who are being brought over.
scriptures: Genesis 8:7
And he sent forth a raven, which went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth.
Genesis 8:14
And in the second month, on the seven and twentieth day of the month, was the earth dried.
Numbers 11:6
But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes.
Joshua 4:23
For the LORD your God dried up the waters of Jordan from before you, until ye were passed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red sea, which he dried up from before us, until we were gone over:
1 Kings 17:7
And it came to pass after a while, that the brook dried up, because there had been no rain in the land.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live danger is Numbers 11:6 — a people whose souls are dried away in the presence of daily provision, because the provision is not the kind they wanted.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is plain and nothing is being contested. What repays attention is the pairing of Joshua 4:23 with Numbers 11:6, since the same generation is in view. God dried the Red sea and later the Jordan — both times to bring a people over, both times commemorated with a memorial and a catechism for children — and the same people said our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes. Manna was bread from heaven, given daily, sufficient, and free, and it was despised because it was ordinary. The parallel to a church that finds the ordinary means of grace insufficiently interesting is exact.

The principle to recover is that God dries streams as well as seas, and both are His work. Elijah had just announced a drought at the word of the LORD and was then sustained beside a brook that the drought itself would kill. When it failed, he was not abandoned but redirected — to a widow in Zidon, to a handful of meal, to a resurrection. The dried brook was the means of the next thing. This is providence at its most uncomfortable and most instructive: the believer is not promised that the stream he was drinking from will not fail, but that the God who dried the Red sea has a reason and a next place.
roots_summary: The Hebrew verb is charab or yabesh, both meaning to be dry or waste; yabbashah, the noun, is the dry land of Genesis 1:9 and of the sea crossings.
roots_lines: Hebrew charab (H2717) — to be dry, waste, desolate; the waters were dried up from off the earth (Genesis 8:7).
Hebrew yabesh (H3001) — to be dry, to wither; the earth dried (Genesis 8:14) and the brook dried up (1 Kings 17:7).
Hebrew yabbashah (H3004) — dry land; the third day of creation (Genesis 1:9) and the ground Israel walked at the sea and the Jordan.
Hebrew yabesh in Numbers 11:6 — our soul is dried away, the same withering verb turned inward on the appetite.
Greek xeraino (G3583) — to dry up, wither; the water thereof was dried up (Revelation 16:12), the last of the Bible’s dried waters.
usage: The LORD your God dried up the waters of Jordan from before you (Joshua 4:23) — the second drying, taught to children beside twelve stones.
Our soul is dried away… beside this manna (Numbers 11:6) — daily bread despised for being ordinary.
The brook dried up, because there had been no rain in the land (1 Kings 17:7) — the failing stream as the means of the next provision.

etymology: Old English sucan. Webster 1828: to draw with the mouth; to draw milk from the breast; to imbibe. In the Authorized Version the word is used plainly of nursing, and then figuratively for drawing sustenance out of unlikely places — honey from a rock, the abundance of the seas, and the wealth of the nations.
biblical_def: Suck begins in the plainest place. Sarah’s wonder is a nursery scene: Who would have said unto Abraham, that Sarah should have given children suck? for I have born him a son in his old age (Genesis 21:7). The harlot before Solomon says when I rose in the morning to give my child suck, behold, it was dead (1 Kings 3:21). Job in his grief asks why the breasts that I should suck? (Job 3:12). From there Scripture makes it a figure for God’s provision in hard places: He made him to suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock (Deuteronomy 32:13), and Zebulun and Issachar shall suck of the abundance of the seas, and of treasures hid in the sand (Deuteronomy 33:19). Isaiah promises the restored city that she shalt suck the milk of the Gentiles, and shalt suck the breast of kings: and thou shalt know that I the LORD am thy Saviour (Isaiah 60:16), and offers the tenderest maternal image in the prophets: that ye may suck, and be satisfied with the breasts of her consolations (Isaiah 66:11). The dark use is Job’s: the wicked shall suck the poison of asps (Job 20:16). What a man draws in is what he lives on, and Scripture asks what that is.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SUCK as to draw with the mouth; to draw milk from the breast; and figuratively, to imbibe, to draw into or absorb. The biblical figure of drawing sustenance from an unlikely source rests on the last sense.
webster_full: SUCK, v.t. — To draw with the mouth; to draw out with the mouth, as a fluid.
To draw milk from the breast with the mouth; as, a child sucks.
To imbibe; to draw into or absorb; as, the earth sucks in the rain.
SUCK, n. — The act of drawing with the mouth; milk drawn from the breast.
The New Testament’s corresponding image is Peter’s: As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby (1 Peter 2:2). The appetite is the point.
scriptures: Genesis 21:7
And she said, Who would have said unto Abraham, that Sarah should have given children suck? for I have born him a son in his old age.
Deuteronomy 32:13
He made him ride on the high places of the earth, that he might eat the increase of the fields; and he made him to suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock;
He shall suck the poison of asps: the viper's tongue shall slay him.
Isaiah 60:16
Thou shalt also suck the milk of the Gentiles, and shalt suck the breast of kings: and thou shalt know that I the LORD am thy Saviour and thy Redeemer, the mighty One of Jacob.
Isaiah 66:11
That ye may suck, and be satisfied with the breasts of her consolations; that ye may milk out, and be delighted with the abundance of her glory.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The loss is a squeamishness about Scripture’s bodily and maternal imagery, which produces preaching thinner and more abstract than the book it comes from.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is now chiefly avoided rather than redefined. Scripture is not embarrassed by the nursing infant, and it uses the image of a mother’s milk for God’s comfort without apology — As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you (Isaiah 66:13), which stands two verses after the promise that His people may suck, and be satisfied with the breasts of her consolations. A pulpit that will not read these verses aloud has decided it is more delicate than the Holy Ghost, and its comfort will be correspondingly abstract.

The principle to recover is the appetite. Deuteronomy 32:13 has God making His people suck honey out of the rock — sustenance drawn from what looks least likely to yield it, which is the wilderness in one image. Peter turns the same picture into the standing duty of a Christian: As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby (1 Peter 2:2). The appetite is commanded, not merely described, and the sincere milk is the word. Job 20:16 gives the alternative in the same verb: a man who feeds on wickedness shall suck the poison of asps. Everyone draws something in. The question Scripture presses is what.
roots_summary: The Hebrew yanaq means to suck or to nurse; its causative means to give suck. The related noun names a suckling child, and Isaiah’s tender plant in chapter 53 comes from the same root.
roots_lines: Hebrew yanaq (H3243) — to suck, to nurse; Genesis 21:7, Deuteronomy 32:13, Isaiah 60:16, 66:11.
Hebrew yoneq (H3126) — a suckling, a young shoot; he shall grow up before him as a tender plant (Isaiah 53:2) uses this root of the Servant.
Hebrew 'olel and yoneq — babes and sucklings, out of whose mouth God ordains strength (Psalm 8:2), quoted by our Lord in Matthew 21:16.
Hebrew mats in Isaiah 66:11 — to drain or milk out; the second verb in that verse, rendered milk out.
Greek thelazo (G2337) — to suckle, to nurse; used in the Gospels of nursing mothers in the day of tribulation (Matthew 24:19).
usage: That Sarah should have given children suck (Genesis 21:7) — the promise kept in the plainest possible scene.
He made him to suck honey out of the rock (Deuteronomy 32:13) — sustenance drawn from what looked least likely to yield it.
He shall suck the poison of asps (Job 20:16) — the same verb turned on the man who feeds upon wickedness.

etymology: From Latin fundare, to lay a bottom or base, from fundus, bottom. Webster 1828: set; established; fixed firmly. In the Authorized Version God is the subject: He founded the earth, He founded Zion, He founded His testimonies for ever — and our Lord ends the Sermon on the Mount with a house founded upon a rock.
biblical_def: Founded in Scripture is what God does that afterwards holds. The creation is described in the verb: he hath founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the floods (Psalm 24:2); as for the world and the fulness thereof, thou hast founded them (Psalm 89:11); The LORD by wisdom hath founded the earth; by understanding hath he established the heavens (Proverbs 3:19). Even the valleys are where He put them — the waters go down by the valleys unto the place which thou hast founded for them (Psalm 104:8). The same verb secures His word: Concerning thy testimonies, I have known of old that thou hast founded them for ever (Psalm 119:152). And it secures His people’s refuge: the LORD hath founded Zion, and the poor of his people shall trust in it (Isaiah 14:32) — a foundation laid, and the poor named as those who take shelter on it. Our Lord closes His great sermon with the word and puts it to a test: the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock (Matthew 7:25). The difference between the two houses is invisible until the storm, and it is entirely below ground.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FOUNDED as set; fixed; established on a basis; and FOUND, as a verb, to lay the basis of anything; to set or place on a permanent basis.
webster_full: FOUND, v.t. [L. fundo, fundare; fundus, bottom.] — To lay the basis of any thing; to set, or place, as on something solid for support.
To begin and build; to lay the foundation and raise a superstructure; as, to found a city.
To establish on a basis; to fix firmly.
FOUNDED, pp. — Set; fixed; established on a basis; begun and built.
Webster’s fixed firmly is the biblical force. A thing founded is not merely started; it is set on something that will bear it, and the whole question in Matthew 7 is what that something is.
scriptures: Psalm 24:2
For he hath founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the floods.
Psalm 89:11
The heavens are thine, the earth also is thine: as for the world and the fulness thereof, thou hast founded them.
Psalm 119:152
Concerning thy testimonies, I have known of old that thou hast founded them for ever.
Isaiah 14:32
What shall one then answer the messengers of the nation? That the LORD hath founded Zion, and the poor of his people shall trust in it.
Matthew 7:25
And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.
corruption_summary: Matthew 7:25 is corrupted when the rock is made anything other than what our Lord says it is — hearing His sayings and doing them — and Psalm 119:152 whenever the permanence of God’s testimonies is traded for the assumption that later ages revise earlier ones.
corruption_paragraphs: Our Lord identifies the rock in the preceding verse: Whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock (Matthew 7:24). The foundation is not sincerity, not religious feeling, not attendance, and not doctrinal knowledge held without obedience — the foolish builder in the parable heard the same sermon. Nor is this works-righteousness: the same chapter has just warned that many will say Lord, Lord and be told I never knew you, so the issue is a real relation to Christ that produces doing. James says it in his own idiom: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves (James 1:22). The storm does not create the difference; it reveals a difference already there and invisible.

Psalm 119:152 is the other foundation and it is under different pressure. Thou hast founded them for ever is said of God’s testimonies, and it is incompatible with the assumption that Scripture’s moral teaching is a record of an earlier stage that later generations improve upon. The historical-critical enterprise, and the progressive theology built on it, both require the testimonies to be founded in a time and revisable with the times. The psalmist says he has known of old that they were founded for ever — and Paul’s foundation language points the same way: other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11), and the foundation of God standeth sure (2 Timothy 2:19).
roots_summary: The Hebrew yasad means to found or establish, and its noun is a foundation; the Greek themelioo in Matthew 7:25 is from themelios, a foundation stone.
roots_lines: Hebrew yasad (H3245) — to found, establish, lay a foundation; Psalm 24:2, 89:11, 119:152; Proverbs 3:19; Isaiah 14:32.
Hebrew mosad and yesod — a foundation; the nouns from the same root, used of the temple and of the earth’s pillars.
Greek themelioo (G2311) — to lay a foundation, to found; it was founded upon a rock (Matthew 7:25), and rooted and grounded in love (Ephesians 3:17).
Greek themelios (G2310) — a foundation stone; other foundation can no man lay (1 Corinthians 3:11), the foundation of God standeth sure (2 Timothy 2:19).
Greek petra (G4073) — a rock, bedrock, as against psammos, sand; the contrast that decides both houses in Matthew 7.
usage: The LORD by wisdom hath founded the earth (Proverbs 3:19) — creation described as a foundation laid.
Thou hast founded them for ever (Psalm 119:152) — God’s testimonies fixed, not revisable by later ages.
It fell not: for it was founded upon a rock (Matthew 7:25) — the difference between two houses is below ground until the storm.

etymology: From Latin magus, through Greek, from the Persian priestly caste. Webster 1828: one skilled in magic; one who practises the black art. In the Authorized Version the magicians are court officials of Egypt and Babylon — professional interpreters and enchanters — and Scripture records exactly where their power stopped.
biblical_def: The magicians in Scripture are a professional class attached to a throne, and their story is a story of a limit. In Egypt they fail Pharaoh from the beginning: I told this unto the magicians; but there was none that could declare it to me (Genesis 41:24). At the exodus they keep pace for a time: they turn rods to serpents, water to blood, and bring up frogs with their enchantments (Exodus 7:11, 22; 8:7). Then comes the third plague and the sentence that ends their career: the magicians did so with their enchantments to bring forth lice, but they could not (Exodus 8:18), and they say to Pharaoh, This is the finger of God (Exodus 8:19). Two plagues later they cannot even stand: the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils; for the boil was upon the magicians (Exodus 9:11). In Babylon the pattern repeats. Daniel and his companions are examined and found ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers that were in all his realm (Daniel 1:20), and in the next chapter the magicians cannot tell the king his dream. Whatever power they had was real enough to deceive and never enough to save.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MAGICIAN as one skilled in magic; one that practises the black art; an enchanter; a necromancer. In Scripture the term names a recognized office in the courts of Egypt and Babylon.
webster_full: MAGICIAN, n. — One skilled in magic; one that practises the black art; an enchanter; a necromancer; a sorcerer or sorceress.
MAGIC, n. — The art or science of putting into action the power of spirits; or the science of producing wonderful effects by the aid of superhuman beings.

Webster does not treat magic as empty conjuring, and neither does Scripture. The Egyptian enchanters produced something; the question the narrative presses is not whether they had power but whose power it was and where it ran out.
scriptures: Genesis 41:24
And the thin ears devoured the seven good ears: and I told this unto the magicians; but there was none that could declare it to me.
Exodus 7:11
Then Pharaoh also called the wise men and the sorcerers: now the magicians of Egypt, they also did in like manner with their enchantments.
Exodus 8:18
And the magicians did so with their enchantments to bring forth lice, but they could not: so there were lice upon man, and upon beast.
Exodus 8:19
Then the magicians said unto Pharaoh, This is the finger of God: and Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he hearkened not unto them; as the LORD had said.
Daniel 1:20
And in all matters of wisdom and understanding, that the king enquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers that were in all his realm.
corruption_summary: The magicians are corrupted in modern reading in opposite directions: reduced to stage conjurors whose tricks Moses merely outperformed, or inflated into evidence that occult power is a match for God’s. Scripture allows neither.
corruption_paragraphs: The rationalizing reading makes the Egyptian magicians illusionists and the plagues a contest of technique. The text will not support it: they turned rods into serpents and water into blood, and the narrative reports it without qualification, adding only that Aaron’s rod swallowed theirs. Paul names two of them by tradition — as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth (2 Timothy 3:8) — and treats them as a type of real opposition rather than of fraud. Scripture’s consistent testimony is that occult power exists, that it is forbidden (Deuteronomy 18:10-12), and that it is genuinely dangerous. Simon in Samaria bewitched the people and had a following before he ever heard the gospel (Acts 8:9).

The opposite error inflates that admission into dualism, as though two comparable powers were contending. Exodus 8:18 settles it in five words: but they could not. The magicians who had matched two plagues could not produce lice, and they said so to Pharaoh’s face — This is the finger of God. Two plagues later they could not stand in Moses’ presence because they were covered in boils. The limit is not a close-run thing. Daniel makes the same point in Babylon by a different route: the magicians could not tell the king his dream, and Daniel says plainly that the secret is not revealed for any wisdom he has more than any living, but there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets (Daniel 2:28).
roots_summary: The Hebrew chartom denotes a sacred scribe or engraver — an official skilled in the priestly writings — and is the word used in both the Egyptian and Babylonian courts; the Greek in Acts is mageuo, to practise magic.
roots_lines: Hebrew chartom (H2748) — a sacred scribe, diviner, magician; the court office in Egypt (Genesis 41:24; Exodus 7:11) and Babylon (Daniel 1:20).
Hebrew lahat and lat — secret arts, enchantments; they also did in like manner with their enchantments (Exodus 7:11).
Hebrew 'etsba' 'elohim — the finger of God; the magicians’ own confession (Exodus 8:19), and the phrase our Lord uses of casting out devils (Luke 11:20).
Greek magos (G3097) — a magus; used both of Simon and Elymas as sorcerers, and of the wise men from the east in Matthew 2.
Greek mageuo (G3096) — to practise magic; Simon, which beforetime in the same city used sorcery (Acts 8:9).
usage: They also did in like manner with their enchantments (Exodus 7:11) — the power is real, and the narrative does not deny it.
The magicians did so with their enchantments to bring forth lice, but they could not (Exodus 8:18) — the limit, reached at the third plague.
Ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers (Daniel 1:20) — the same contest run again in Babylon, with the same outcome.
